units.title: Learning the laundry room
units.instruction: Read the complete passage. Use each word at most once; five words are not needed.

materials.title: Learning the laundry room
materials.text:
For many students, moving into accommodation means learning to use unfamiliar washing ____1____. At home, somebody else may have selected a programme or dealt with a leaking pipe. In a ____2____ laundry room, personal habits also affect the people who use the space next.

Start by checking the small ____3____ sewn into your clothes. These may specify temperatures or warn against a particular method of cleaning. Then read the ____4____ beside the machine, which explain the sequence of buttons to press. Similar-looking controls do not necessarily work in the same way.

The amount a machine is designed to hold is its ____5____. Packing in more than that amount is not a useful way to save money. Leave enough room for clothes to move, and use an appropriate quantity of detergent. More soap does not automatically produce cleaner clothes.

You may need to ____6____ items that require different treatment, rather than putting everything into one wash. A fabric that tolerates heat well may share a basket with something that does not. The result of ignoring that difference can be permanent ____7____.

When the cycle ends, return promptly to ____8____ your clothes. An occupied machine may look busy even when it has finished, leaving another resident unsure whether it can be used. Check the room's arrangements for items left behind rather than assuming you may leave yours there indefinitely.

Cleaning filters and reporting faults ____9____ can keep a communal service working. A machine is truly ____10____ to the next person only when it is both free and ready for use. Doing laundry is an ordinary task, but sharing the equipment makes small acts of consideration particularly visible.

questions.explanation: Washing machines are the apparatus with programmes and pipes. Labels and instructions provide information, not the apparatus; the other entries cannot name this plural equipment.
Shared fits a room used by several residents. Familiar concerns recognition, available readiness and unsuitable poor fitness; they do not establish communal use. Other words have wrong roles.
Labels are small physical tags sewn into clothing. Instructions may be printed on them but are not themselves the sewn tags; machines are too large and other nouns abstract.
Instructions explain the sequence of controls, as the following clause states. Labels name the sewn tags already mentioned, while debate is discussion and capacity/damage are not directions.
Capacity is explicitly defined as the amount designed to be held. Damage is harm, debate discussion and machines/labels physical things; the remaining entries do not name the quantity limit.

Separate means divide items needing different treatments. Remove takes something out but does not establish distinct washes; prevent needs a prevented event and other entries are not suitable base verbs.
Permanent damage is lasting harm caused by incorrect treatment. Capacity is a limit and debate an exchange of views; other nouns do not name this negative result.

Remove means take the finished clothes out so another resident can use the machine. Separate divides clothing by type but need not empty the machine; prevent does not name collection. Other entries do not fit.
Regularly describes recurring maintenance and reports. Loosely describes a manner of attachment, not a sensible maintenance frequency; other entries do not fill the adverb slot.
Available is defined by free and ready for use. Familiar means known, shared communal, unsuitable unfit; none expresses readiness for the next person. The remaining words have inappropriate roles.

units.title: Finding time for a rehearsal
units.instruction: Read the complete passage. Use each word at most once; five words are not needed.

materials.title: Finding time for a rehearsal
materials.text:
A student orchestra needed a rehearsal schedule that could accommodate both the performers and the rooms they used. The organiser initially treated each player's free hours as an independent preference. In practice, the relevant ____1____ were connected: a percussionist might be free while the only room large enough for the instruments was not.

The first task was to identify what was ____2____. A rehearsal of the full orchestra required particular players, suitable space and access to the instruments. Other arrangements were more ____3____. A section could sometimes practise separately, and a short discussion about interpretation did not necessarily require the largest hall.

The organiser proposed several ____4____ rather than circulating one supposedly ideal timetable. Musicians could then explain which difficulties each proposal created. This made the ____5____ involved more visible: gaining an extra hour in the large hall might require some players to alter an existing commitment.

Fairness did not mean giving every player an identical schedule. Their roles and practical needs were not identical. It did mean making the reasons for each ____6____ clear, so an inconvenient decision was not mistaken for simple neglect.

After discussion, the group reached a ____7____ that nobody considered perfect but everyone could use. They also built in a small ____8____ between sessions. Without that spare time, one late finish would delay the next group's preparation.

The resulting plan was ____9____ to change if a room became unavailable. Its purpose was coordination, not prediction of a flawless term. Keeping that distinction ____10____ helped the orchestra respond to problems without treating every adjustment as evidence that planning had failed. A useful schedule represented an agreement about how to proceed, together with a way to reconsider it.

questions.explanation: Constraints are connected limits on players, room and equipment. Preferences are personal wishes but cannot cover room availability; obstacles are impediments rather than the linked scheduling conditions as a whole. Other entries do not name the system’s limits as precisely.

Essential describes requirements that must hold for a full rehearsal. Flexible describes changeability, identical sameness, rigid inflexibility and uniform consistency; none means required for this activity. Other words lack adjective function here.

Flexible contrasts with required full-orchestra conditions and is illustrated by different feasible formats. Rigid reverses that; identical/uniform deny variation, while explicit concerns disclosure and essential necessity.

Alternatives are several possible timetables offered for discussion. Allocations are distributions, constraints limits and preferences desires; none identifies the proposed different plans as directly. Buffer and compromise are singular.

Trade-offs express gaining hall time at the cost of changing another commitment. Obstacles name difficulties but not the exchanged advantage/cost relationship; preferences and constraints do not name the balance involved.

Allocation assigns scarce rehearsal resources, with reasons given to those affected. Compromise is the later overall settlement, buffer spare time, and alternatives are proposed plans rather than each distribution decision.

A compromise is an imperfect but usable agreement reached through discussion. Allocation may assign resources without agreement; a buffer is spare time. The remaining bank entries do not identify the negotiated settlement.
A buffer is spare time between sessions absorbing overruns. Compromise is agreement and allocation assignment; obstacles and preferences are plural and not time margins. Other entries do not fit.

Subject to change is the established phrase for revisability. Rigid would contradict it and other adjectives do not take to change in this meaning. Uniform/identical describe sameness rather than contingency.

Explicit means the distinction is made clear. Flexible describes adaptability, essential necessity and rigid inflexibility; none names clear disclosure. Other entries do not complete keeping the distinction with this meaning.

units.title: The unopened envelope
units.instruction: Use the word in brackets to form one word that fits each gap in the complete passage.

materials.title: The unopened envelope
materials.text:
The ____1____ (DISCOVER) of an unopened envelope behind a drawer led to an ____2____ (EXPECT) visit. I did not recognise the name on the front. Out of ____3____ (CURIOUS), I asked my aunt whether she recognised it.

She explained that the envelope belonged to the previous occupant of the house. There was no ____4____ (PERSON) connection between the writer and our family. We therefore left it sealed while she contacted the former resident through the letting agent.

When he came to collect it, he opened it himself and invited us to look at the card inside. He unfolded it ____5____ (CARE), taking time not to tear its delicate paper edges. It contained a drawing his sister had made as a child, not the formal document I had imagined.

The ____6____ (REAL) that such a small object could matter so much changed my view of it. Its ____7____ (ORIGIN) owner saw a family memory where I had seen a puzzle. Finding something did not give me a right to settle every question about it. His visit revealed a ____8____ (POSSIBLE) I had not considered: a forgotten object could mean far more to its owner than to the finder.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 1 with one word formed from DISCOVER.
questions.explanation: The discovery of an unopened envelope requires the event noun discovery. Discover is a verb and discoverable an adjective.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 2 with one word formed from EXPECT.
questions.explanation: An unexpected visit describes the unforeseen outcome of finding the envelope. Expectation is a noun and unexpectedly an adverb, so neither modifies visit here.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 3 with one word formed from CURIOUS.
questions.explanation: Out of curiosity requires the noun curiosity. Curious and curiously are adjective/adverb forms.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 4 with one word formed from PERSON.
questions.explanation: A personal connection modifies the noun connection with an adjective. Personally is adverb and personality noun.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 5 with one word formed from CARE.
questions.explanation: Carefully modifies unfolded; careful/careless are adjectives. The explicit concern not to tear excludes carelessly.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 6 with one word formed from REAL.
questions.explanation: The realisation/realization that requires a noun naming a new understanding, with both spellings accepted. Verbs and adjective do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 7 with one word formed from ORIGIN.
questions.explanation: The original owner uses an adjective identifying the initial owner. Origin is noun and originally adverb.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 8 with one word formed from POSSIBLE.
questions.explanation: A possibility requires a singular count noun for the idea newly considered. Possible is an adjective and possibly an adverb.
